That only works if the seed controls all of that randomness. This method evaluates the full table twice with the same seed and warns if the results differ, which is worth checking before a long run. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : The seed to evaluate with. By default, it's the `seed=` of the ablation. [tolerance]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[0.0]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : The largest difference in a metric that still counts as the same. Differences from floating-point rounding (e.g., from a model that sums its trees in parallel, in whichever order they finish) always count as the same: these are relative differences of up to `1e-9`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if both evaluations gave the same metrics (within `tolerance=`), `False` (with a warning that lists the metrics that differ) if they didn't. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Here's an `evaluate()` function that forgets to use its seed, so that its bootstrap sample is different every time. ::: {#e10d94ed .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import warnings import pointblank as pb import polars as pl temps = [20 + (k * 37 % 11 - 5) * 0.6 for k in range(300)] readings = pl.DataFrame({"temp": temps}) def evaluate(train, *, seed): sample = train.sample(fraction=1.0, with_replacement=True) return abs(sample["temp"].mean() - 20) validation = ( pb.Validate(data=readings) .col_vals_between(columns="temp", left=-10, right=45) .interrogate() ) ablation = pb.Ablation(validation, evaluate=evaluate) with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught: warnings.simplefilter("always") deterministic = ablation.check_determinism() print(deterministic) print(caught[0].message) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` False `evaluate=` isn't deterministic: given the full table and the seed 0 twice, it returned different results (score: 0.10199999999999676 and 0.12800000000000367). Use the seed for every source of randomness in training, or the ablation's comparisons will be noisier than they need to be. ``` ::: ::: Passing `seed=seed` to `sample()` would fix it, and the check would then return `True`.
